bp: Most web and enterprise decisions are made from structured data: rows and columns about users, products, transactions, dates, prices, clicks, forecasts, and business events. Recommendation systems, demand forecasts, user behavior analysis, and decision-support dashboards all depend on models that can read this kind of organized record and predict something useful. The usual pattern is local: for each table, engineers clean the columns, train a model for that one task, tune it, and repeat the process when a new table or business question appears. This tutorial asks whether structured data can move toward a more general kind of model. Instead of starting from an empty model for every dataset, a generalist model would arrive with prior experience from many structured tasks and adapt from a few examples or instructions. The need is practical: organizations have many related tables, but building a separate predictive machine for each one wastes work and fails to reuse common structure.
wh: Structured data is hard to generalize across because tables look simple on the surface but mean different things underneath. One column may be an age, another may be a product category, another may be a timestamp, and another may be a sparse count of rare events. The same number can mean money in one table and a risk score in another. Conventional methods work well when trained for a fixed dataset because they can learn that dataset's column meanings, value ranges, missingness patterns, and target label. The difficulty appears when the goal shifts from one dataset to many. A model that learned one company's customer table may not know how to treat a medical table, a sales table, or a web activity table. The tutorial's central tension is therefore transfer: how can a model reuse what is common across structured prediction while still respecting the local meaning of each new table?
naive: A smart beginner would train a strong model separately for every structured task. For a recommendation table, train one predictor; for forecasting, train another; for user behavior analysis, train another. This works when there is enough labeled data, time, and expertise for each task. It fails when tasks are numerous, labels are scarce, or the user wants a model to handle a new table without a full training cycle. The beginner might next copy recipes from language foundation models, but that also fails as a simple answer: words arrive in sequences with shared grammar, while tables have changing column names, value types, missing entries, and task definitions.
ap: The core idea is to treat structured modeling as something that may have reusable foundations, not only isolated dataset-specific tricks. The tutorial surveys the old toolkit, including linear-style predictors, tree-based boosting, and deep structured networks, then places them beside newer structured foundation models. A foundation model here means a large model first trained on many tasks so it can carry general habits into a new task. In-context learning means showing the model a small set of examples from the new table so it can infer what prediction is being asked for without changing all its internal settings. Synthetic data generation means creating artificial but task-shaped tables to broaden what the model sees during preparation. The central move is not one new algorithm; it is a map of how pretraining, multi-task learning, generated data, and example-based adaptation might make structured data models more universal.
mech: The mechanism begins with many structured settings rather than one table. The model is exposed to varied records that stand in for recommendation, forecasting, user behavior analysis, and other predictive tasks. Each task gives it examples of inputs, such as rows with fields, and desired outputs, such as a rating, a future value, a class, or a decision signal. During large-scale pretraining, the model is pushed to discover reusable operations: notice which fields help, handle missing values, compare rows, track repeated patterns, and infer what target is being predicted. Synthetic data can enlarge this training world by generating additional tables with controlled shapes, so the model sees more combinations than a single company or benchmark would provide. At use time, a new table arrives. Instead of training a fresh model from scratch, the system receives a few examples or task descriptions in context. Those examples show which columns matter, what the output means, and how inputs map to answers. The model then produces predictions or decisions for new rows. The tutorial also covers the unresolved design choices: how to build useful generated data, how to define pretraining objectives, how to combine multiple tasks without confusion, and how to evaluate whether the model truly transfers rather than merely fitting familiar cases.
math: The main mathematical ideas are learning from examples, transfer across tasks, probability under uncertainty, and objective design. Learning from examples means finding a rule that maps observed input fields to an output, then reusing that rule on unseen rows. Transfer means asking which parts of that rule are local and which parts are general. For structured data, the general parts may include comparing rows, detecting which columns carry signal, treating missing entries carefully, and estimating how repeated patterns predict future behavior. Probability matters because the model rarely knows the answer with certainty; it is estimating likely ratings, future values, or user actions from incomplete evidence. Objective design means deciding what counts as wrong during preparation. A pretraining objective is the practice problem the model solves before deployment. If the practice problems match real structured tasks, the learned habits may transfer. If they are poorly chosen, the model may learn shortcuts that look good in tests but fail on new tables. Multi-task learning is the balancing act: train on many tasks so shared structure becomes visible, while preventing one task type from washing out the others.
dots: This paper connects several recurring conference ideas because structured tables sit underneath many application areas. Recommendation papers ask which item should be shown to a user; forecasting papers ask what will happen next; user behavior papers ask what a person is likely to do from past traces. All three are versions of learning a useful rule from organized records. It also connects to ranking, because recommendation and decision support often reduce to sorting candidates by expected usefulness. It connects to probability because a row of data is partial evidence, not a guarantee. It connects to efficiency because adapting from examples could save repeated training cycles. It neighbors language-model work through in-context learning, but the tutorial's theme is different: tables are not free-form text, so the model must understand column roles, value types, and task definitions. The broader field question is whether web-scale structured prediction can gain the flexibility that general models brought to text.
ww: The approach should work when there really are repeated structures across different tables. Many structured tasks, despite different column names, ask similar questions: which signals matter, how strong is each signal, how should missing values be treated, and how should evidence from several fields be combined into a prediction. A model trained across many such tasks can learn these habits before seeing the next dataset. In-context examples then serve as a small translation key. They tell the model that, in this new table, these columns are inputs, this value is the target, and this pattern of rows should produce that kind of answer. That is better than the naive separate-model approach when the cost of starting over is high or when labeled data is limited. Synthetic data may help because it can create controlled practice cases that expose the model to rare table shapes. The reason is not magic scale; it is reuse. The model carries over ordinary structured reasoning and only has to learn the local task framing.
po: The payoff is a roadmap for making structured data modeling more adaptable. Grounded in the abstract, the tutorial helps participants understand established methods, current structured foundation model advances, and open research challenges. The capability it points toward is a model that can support recommendation, forecasting, user behavior analysis, and other structured tasks with less dataset-specific training. It also clarifies what the community still needs: better data generation, clearer multi-task settings, stronger pretraining objectives, and fair evaluation standards. For practitioners, the value is knowing when conventional models remain strong and where generalist structured models may eventually reduce repeated engineering work.
limits: The abstract is a tutorial overview, not a report of a single tested system, so it does not prove that a generalist structured model is already reliable across domains. The input text is also truncated, which limits what can be inferred about the full tutorial scope. The approach assumes that useful common patterns exist across structured datasets and that pretraining examples represent future tasks well enough. It also assumes in-context examples are clear and not misleading. Open questions named in the abstract, including data generation, multi-task setting, pretraining objectives, and evaluation standards, are real limits rather than finished details.
